activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Edouard pushed through the art room door with his backpack still on one shoulder, and the first thing he heard was Gurshan shouting, "It's a tree, obviously. I painted the trunk."

The after-school club had spent three weeks on a surprise exhibit for the school lobby, and each member had been given one panel to decorate behind a curtain, so nobody would spoil the surprise. Now the curtain was coming down, and the room had split into corners. Gurshan stood by his panel of a thick grey column. Elie had painted something flat and floppy and swore it was a fan. A third kid, whose panel showed two curved shapes like tree branches, argued it had to be a snake. Only the club advisor, Mr. Shevchenko, stood quietly by the window, sipping tea.

"We're supposed to assemble them into one thing tomorrow," Elie said, "and it's impossible. The panels don't go together at all."

Edouard wanted the assembly job. He had missed the painting weeks because of a hygiene unit in gym that his mother insisted he finish before rejoining clubs, so tomorrow was his only chance to lead something. He walked the line of panels slowly, like a detective in a show, letting his eyes move from the column to the fan to the snake. He could not see the whole thing directly, because there wasn't one yet, but he began testing an idea in his head. What if the column wasn't a tree trunk? What if it was a leg?

"Gurshan," he said, "stand your panel next to the floppy one."

"Why?"

"Just do it."

Gurshan dragged it over. The flat shape hung beside the column, and Edouard tilted his head. Elie came closer, then the third kid, then two others whose panels showed a wall and a rope. Somebody held up the rope one next to the snake, and someone else propped the wall behind everything. Slowly the pieces governed the shape of the whole, the way a frame decides where a picture can go. When the last panel, an opaque grey sheet that a shy kid had painted without knowing what it was, went up near the top, Elie whispered, "Oh. It's an elephant."

Mr. Shevchenko set his tea down. "You've just acted out something old," he said, but he offered nothing more, which was his way.

Edouard pulled out his phone, and after a minute of searching he read aloud. "It's called a parable. The blind men and the elephant, from ancient India. People each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently." He looked up. "That's us. Each of us saw one piece and thought it was the whole thing."

"So the exhibit is the parable itself," Gurshan said slowly. "The panels go together because they don't match."

"We don't take the curtain down tomorrow," Edouard said. "We put it up, with a gap in the middle, and let people lean through and touch one panel each."

Elie grinned and reached for the roll of grey cloth. "Where do we cut the hole?"

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
Charlotte had one week to finish her cell diagram, and the school microscope was booked solid until the deadline, which was why she stood at the rickety table in the community garden's tool shed holding half an onion and a borrowed slide.

Mr. Joseph, who ran the garden and owned the old brass microscope, had left a note taped to the case: "Bulbs are in the crate by the door. Focus slowly. The thing you want is in the middle. Joseph." She read it twice, then set to work peeling a paper-thin layer of skin from the onion's flesh with tweezers and a steadiness she did not feel. Josephine had offered to come, but Josephine was biased toward the easy version of everything and would probably say the slide was fine when it wasn't. Charlotte wanted her analysis of the cells to be right, not quick.

The shed smelled of soil and damp wood. She lowered the objective lens a hair at a time, and then the field of view bloomed into pale bricks, cell walls stacked like a honeycomb, each one boxed in. The wall she could label from memory. The membrane she found by tracing the faint inner edge, hugging the wall like a second skin. Then she saw it, a darker dot hanging in one cell, and another in the next. She drew them, then paused. Who had first looked at something like this and decided that little dark spot mattered enough to name?

Diana appeared at the shed door with a watering can and a clipboard of bean-patch measurements. "Did it work?" she asked.

"There's a dot in every cell," Charlotte said. "I have to label it, and I don't even know who noticed it first."

Diana set down the can. "My uncle talks about that. The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells." She shrugged. "He was looking at flowers, not onions, and he still saw it."

Charlotte wrote the name on her diagram, then, to make sure she had it, paraphrased it back: "Brown, 1831, orchids. First to describe the nucleus." Diana nodded and pointed at the slide. "Don't move the stage, I want to see."

The deadline was tomorrow, and the drawing would take all evening, which meant giving up the movie with Josephine. Charlotte spent the last of the light shading each nucleus, checking the slide again and again until the shed went dim and she had to work by the door. When she finally packed up, she left a note of her own under Mr. Joseph's, next to the half onion.

"Found the thing in the middle," it said. "Your microscope is better than the school's. Can I come back when we do leaf cells?"

She stuck the pen in her pocket, tucked the diagram inside her jacket where the drizzle couldn't touch it, and ran for the gate.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast.
story:
Charles stood in the kitchen holding a hair dryer, two thermometers, and a bag of rice, which was a strange way to start a Thursday. He had to explain monsoons to his class on Monday, and Ms. Reddy had said his first draft sounded "like a dictionary with a headache." Jaycob was coming over to help, mostly because Jaycob's mother had banned him from the trampoline until his science grade improved.

"Okay," Charles said, laying out his supplies. "The land heats up faster than the ocean in summer. Hot air rises over the land, and wet ocean air rushes in to take its place. That's the principle. When that wet air rises and cools, boom, rain." Jaycob picked up the bag of rice and looked skeptical. "What's this for?" "Props," Charles said. "Rice farming in South Asia needs the monsoon rain. Without it, the fields dry out."

While Jaycob aimed the hair dryer at a tray of dry dirt next to a tray of water, Charles called his grandmother in Kerala on the tablet. She appeared in her kitchen, fanning herself with a newspaper. "Amma, when does the rain usually arrive where you are?" She laughed. "June 1. Every year my calendar has a circle on June 1. The India Meteorological Department says that is the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, right here on our coast. We plan the planting around it." She held up the calendar so he could see the fat red circle. "Your grandfather used to start perspiring from worry two weeks early. I told him, the rain has never read your calendar."

Charles wrote down the date, then checked his trays. The dry dirt read thirty-one degrees; the water tray sat stubbornly at twenty-six. "See? Land heats faster. The ocean stays cooler, so the pressure is different, and the wind blows from the sea toward the land." Jaycob grinned. "So the hair dryer is the sun." "The hair dryer is the sun," Charles agreed solemnly, "and you are a very large cloud."

By the time Matilda arrived to hear a practice run, Charles had taped a map of South Asia to the refrigerator and drawn a fat blue arrow sweeping up from the ocean toward Kerala. Matilda wanted to be the one who ended the presentation, because she had a dramatic closing line ready and had been rehearsing it in the mirror. Charles let her, and she delivered it with both arms raised: "So when the wind changes direction, a whole subcontinent gets out its umbrella." Charles stood beside her, feeling genuinely optimistic for the first time since Thursday. Then Jaycob accidentally knocked the rice off the counter, and all three of them knelt on the kitchen floor, picking up grains and laughing, while the map fluttered gently against the fridge door.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Beak size is inherited, so after the 1977 drought the survivors' offspring had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought.
story:
Kayla sat on the flat rock at the edge of Miller Pond with her science notebook open on her knees. On the page she had drawn two finches, one with a stubby beak and one with a longer one, and she had written "1977" between them with a big question mark. Ms. Tang had assigned a short talk about the finches on the distant islands, and Kayla was stuck. She knew there had been a drought, and she knew the beaks were different afterward, but she could not picture how a dry year could change a bird's beak.

Jensen came down the path with his fishing rod and a granola bar he was boycotting because it had raisins in it. He dropped onto the grass beside her. "Still homework, even out here?"

"It's the finch thing," Kayla said. "I keep thinking the drought must have changed the birds somehow, like it bent their beaks." She flicked a pebble into the pond and watched the rings spread out and fade.

That night, flipping through her family photo album, she stopped at a picture of her dad at age twelve. He had her nose, exactly, the same little bump at the bridge. Her grandfather, in an older photo, had it too. The nose had been handed down, like a keychain her dad kept on his dresser, a brass-colored alloy that had belonged to his own father. Kayla sat very still. Beaks could be handed down the same way, from parent bird to chick. The drought did not bend anything. It just decided which birds lived.

The next afternoon she brought Julius to the pond to test her idea. "Pretend the grass seeds are the small seeds, and these are the big, tough ones," she said, scattering sunflower seeds and pebbles near the rock. Julius used tweezers as a small beak and she used pliers as a large beak. In their drought round, the small seeds were gone, and only the big ones were left. His tweezers barely cracked them; her pliers managed fine. "So the big-beaked birds survived," Julius said slowly, "and then their babies got big beaks from them."

"Right," Kayla said. "After the 1977 drought, the survivors' chicks had larger beaks on average than the birds before it, because beak size runs in families, like my dad's nose." She pulled out her notebook and wrote "inherited" in careful letters. "I'll do the tweezers and pliers for the class. Ms. Tang can be the judge, but I want the numbers to be only approximate, since it's a demonstration, not a real island." Julius grinned and flicked the last sunflower seed into the pond, where a duck scooped it up in one quick, efficient snap.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
Ella sat at the kitchen table glaring at her phone, where eighteen messages to her best friend Edison had gone unanswered for two days. Not one reply, not even a thumbs-up, and Finn had texted her a photo from Saturday showing Edison at the arcade with everybody, including people Edison claimed he couldn't stand. The steam from the kettle rose, and droplets began to condense on the cold window, streaking the glass. Ella wiped it with her sleeve and thought. Edison had ignored her, lied to her, and replaced her, probably. Probably. She chewed her thumbnail. It was possible his phone was broken, but that felt like the kind of excuse people condense into one neat word to escape trouble.

She decided to run a test, the way they did in science. If Edison were truly dumping her as a friend, Finn would know; friends told friends that kind of thing first, like a secret tariff paid on gossip. Ella called him. "Has Edison said anything about me?" she asked, trying to sound casual and landing somewhere near interrogation. "Anything weird?"

"Weird how?" said Finn. "He said his phone died Friday and he's grounded until his mom buys a new charger because he keeps losing them. Oh, and he got sick of the arcade a month ago and only went because his cousin was visiting. He called it 'hostile attribution bias' when his cousin assumed the arcade picked his pocket on purpose. It was just his own holey pocket." Finn paused. "Why, what did you do?"

"Nothing," said Ella, feeling her ears go hot. "Thanks." She hung up and stared at the window. Edison hadn't answered because his phone was dead, and he'd gone to the arcade for a cousin, not to shove Ella out of the picture. She had taken two unclear things and decided they were aimed at her, like an arrow with her name on it, when they were really just a holey pocket and a lost charger.

She marched to Edison's house and knocked. He opened the door holding a bag of chips, his phone dark as a brick in his other hand. "You're talking to me again?" he said. "Great, because I've been going crazy without anyone to argue with. My mom and my cousin are unanimous, they both say I'm dramatic, which is deeply unfair."

"I'm sorry I assumed you were ignoring me on purpose," Ella said. "It was a whole conspiracy in my head. There were charts."

"Naturally," said Edison, holding out the bag. "Chip tariff is one joke about my dramatic personality."

"Deal." She took a chip, stepped inside, and her sneaker skidded on the glossy hallway floor so that she bashed her shoulder into the wall. Edison grinned down at her. "On purpose," he said.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Payton knelt in the garden behind Ms. Ramírez's fence and counted the bites out loud. "Five bean leaves gone, three chewed down to the stem." Something had been eating the seedlings every night, but it never showed itself. She had a hypothesis, which was a word she'd picked to mean a guess you could actually test: she guessed rabbits.

"Rabbits," said Ariah, crouching beside her. "Or slugs. Slugs would be grosser." Ariah wanted the beans for a salad she was planning to bring to the family picnic on Saturday, so every missing leaf felt personal to her.

Last summer, Payton remembered, Ms. Ramírez had lost a whole row of lettuce overnight and blamed deer, though nobody ever saw one. That time there had been no test at all, just blame. Payton didn't want to guess wrong like that. "Here's the plan," she said. "We put out two trays of bean seedlings, exactly the same. We fence one with chicken wire and leave the other open. If the fenced one survives and the open one gets eaten, rabbits win. If both get eaten, it's something that slips through."

They set the trays in the shade, since Ms. Ramírez said afternoon sun would fry one side of the garden, and Payton watered both trays with the same amount from the same cup. "It has to be a fair test," she said. "Everything stays the same except the fence. Same amount of water, same spot so they're the same temperature, and we check both trays at the same times, morning and evening."

The first morning, the open tray was chewed to nubs and the fenced tray was untouched. "Rabbits," Ariah said, almost sadly. But Payton noticed something the rabbits supposedly couldn't transmit to anyone: slimy trails, silver lines looping across both trays, straight through the chicken wire and back out. Her hypothesis was wrong, and the wrongness was the most useful thing she'd found all week. "Slugs," she said. "They fit through the holes."

Ms. Ramírez brought out two saucers of beer from her kitchen, because she'd heard slugs crawled into it and never crawled out, and she set one saucer by each tray. "Same amount in each," she said, handing Payton the bottle, "and we'll look together, both trays, right after dinner." It seemed inevitable that by Saturday the slugs would win anyway, that the salad would be lettuce and disappointment.

But Saturday morning, both saucers were full of slugs and both trays of beans stood whole and green. Ariah picked a handful of pods for her salad, and Payton wrote in her notebook, "Hypothesis overturned once, supported once. Fencing kept out nothing that mattered. Beer saucers for the win." Then she looked up and saw Ms. Ramírez's fat speckled hen calmly hopping the fence, landing in the lettuce, and settling in to feast on the very slugs climbing the remaining leaves. Ariah raised her cup of water toward the hen. "Assistant gardener," she said, "you're hired."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Oliver's cue card was sweating in his hand along with the rest of him. Ms. Patel had brought the whole class for the student charter presentations, and each of them had to read a right from the Canadian Charter and explain it in their own words in front of a real judge. Oliver had drawn section 2, freedom of expression, and he had rehearsed it so many times on the bus that Tessa had threatened to sit somewhere else.

"I still don't get why we had to invest a whole month in this," Ryden whispered as they filed into the wooden benches. "It's just a bunch of words on a wall."

"It's not just words," Oliver said, though privately the words had started to swim together.

Before the presentations began, the judge invited questions, and Ryden's hand shot up. "If we have freedom of expression," Ryden asked, "does that mean anyone can say anything they want? Anywhere?"

A boy from another school, sitting two rows ahead, nodded hard. "That's what it means. You can't get in trouble for saying stuff."

"Not exactly," Tessa said. She'd flipped to the front of her copy of the Charter, where a chart laid out the sections. She stood up so the visiting rows could hear her. "It says here that the rights are subject to reasonable limits, limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. That's section one."

"Reasonable limits," the judge repeated, and smiled like someone who had spent a career inside that sentence.

Oliver sat very still. He stared at his cue card, at the big number 2 he'd written at the top, and a question formed that he actually wanted answered. If section 1 came before section 2, then the rights weren't a wall you could hide behind. They were more like a net, one that held but had give in it. He tested the idea against things he knew: the school banning slurs, the fire alarm prank last spring, his grandfather's stories about marching. It fit. It fit everything.

When his name was called, he left the cue card on the bench. He stood at the small podium, saw the judge's pen hovering, and explained freedom of expression in his own words: it meant you could say what you believed, but the saying wasn't untouchable, because someone had to be able to show the limit made sense. He used the phrase "reasonable limits" once, then pushed it aside and talked about the group chat where someone had posted a cruel joke and claimed it was free speech, and how everyone had known, somehow, that this wasn't what free speech was for.

Afterward Ms. Patel told him his delivery was resilient, that he'd recovered from dropping his notes halfway through like a professional. He was still catching his breath when Tessa elbowed him.

"So next year," she said, "when we do the mock trial team, you're auditioning. No arguments."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
Emilia had one week left before she left for Camp Wyoka, and one problem she could not stop chewing on: she was the only girl in her grade who had never spent a night away from home. Nevaeh had gone last summer and sent back a postcard with a smudge of lake water on it. Roy had gone twice and claimed the food was better than his mom's, which nobody believed. Emilia wanted to arrive with something, anything, that made her feel less like the new kid.

So she had begun a campaign. First she petitioned her mother for a sleeping bag rated for cold nights, even though August would be warm, because it looked experienced. Her mother agreed on one condition, a settlement of sorts: Emilia would also take the flashlight, the whistle, and the ugly rain poncho, no arguing. Emilia shook on it in the kitchen, feeling like she had won something and lost something at the same time.

The second problem came up on Tuesday, when Roy stopped by with his duffel bag already packed, eleven days early. "There's no wifi at the dock," he said, sprawled on her porch steps. "Nevaeh says the older campers lie out there at night and dare the new kids to find north without a phone." He grinned. "Nevaeh failed. She pointed at a boat."

That night Emilia lay on the picnic table in the backyard, phone dark beside her, staring up. She remembered a page from the camp booklet, a diagram with a bold diagonal line drawn across a pattern of stars. She found the Dipper, then tried the line herself. The two stars at the outer edge of the bowl, the ones farthest from the handle, seemed to aim somewhere, so she walked the line with her eyes until she hit a lone, stubborn star that didn't twinkle much.

"That one has to be Polaris," she said out loud, to nobody. She did it three more times, starting over each time, and every time she landed on the same star. She checked it against her phone compass only once, at the very end, holding her breath. North.

The last week passed in a blur of packing. Then came the letter, four days into camp, which her mother read aloud at the kitchen table:

Dear Mom, the food is fine. Tell Roy the canoe did not flip, it only leaned. Last night we lay on the dock and Nevaeh said the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl point to Polaris, the North Star. I found it first. They made me do it again with my eyes closed, which is cheating, and I still found it. Tonight they want to try finding south, and Nevaeh says she knows a way, but she won't tell us what it is.

Love, Emilia

Her mother set the letter down and looked out at the dark backyard for a while. Then she picked up a pen and the next sheet of paper.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Vincent had been at the community art studio for forty minutes, and his drawing of a honeybee still looked like a smudge with wings. The assignment from Mr. Moose was "values," which meant making some parts of the paper almost white and other parts nearly black, with everything in between. Vincent's problem was the in-between. His dark areas went fine, but when he tried to make a pale gray, the pencil suddenly stopped cooperating.

"Your bee looks like it flew through a chimney," said Fox, leaning over from the next easel.

"Thanks. Really helpful." Vincent held up two pencils that looked almost identical, same yellow paint, same eraser, same length. One of them laid down a rich, velvety gray. The other one barely marked the paper at all, no matter how hard he pressed. He had been assuming he was pressing wrong, or the paper was bad, or his hand was having a bad day. But now he lined up the marks side by side and frowned. Same hand, same paper, same pressure. Two very different results.

"That's weird," said Richard, who had come over to steal one of Fox's lemon candies. "They're the same kind of pencil."

Vincent got an idea. He turned both pencils sideways and scratched a thick patch with each one, then pressed his thumbnail into the patches. The dark pencil's mark smeared and felt almost waxy, like it wanted to slide around. The light one's mark stayed put and felt firm, even a little brittle, like dried mud. He scratched the wood near the end of the dark one, where the paint was chipped, and looked at the core inside. Then he found an old broken pencil in the scrap bin with a similar core and compared them. The cores were different colors, one shinier and blacker, one duller and grayer.

"Guys, I think the stuff inside isn't the same," Vincent said. "I bet it's graphite powder mixed with clay." He pointed at the duller core. "This one has more clay in it. That's why it's harder, and harder pencils leave lighter marks."

"So the pencil's not broken, it's just bossy," said Fox.

Mr. Moose wandered by with his coffee and looked at Vincent's test patches. "Now you're thinking like an artist and a scientist at the same time." He sipped his coffee like it was nectar and moved on without saying anything else, which Vincent appreciated.

Vincent hunted through the studio's pencil drawer and found a handful of different ones. He made a strip of test marks across the bottom of his paper, light to dark, and taped it to the corner of his easel like a menu. Then he redrew the bee, using the hard, clay-heavy pencils for the pale wing edges and the soft ones for the shadow under its fuzzy body. It finally looked like a bee, hovering there, ready to consume a flower.

"Better," Fox admitted. "Less chimney."

Vincent grinned and started a second bee.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
story:
Theodore's grandfather had made the offer at dinner on Sunday, and it had been sitting in Theodore's head like a stone ever since. Give me your thousand dollars, the old man had said, and I'll hold it for five years at five percent simple interest. When you finish eighth grade, you get it back with the interest. His mother called it generous. Theodore called it suspicious. Nobody hands over free money without a catch.

On Monday he cornered Louane by the lockers. "Five percent of a thousand is fifty a year," he said. "Five years, that's two hundred fifty. I get back one thousand two hundred fifty."

"So what's the problem?"

"Mr. Janssen said compound interest makes money grow faster. My grandfather said simple. One of them is shorting me." He flipped open his notebook, where he had copied the numbers in careful columns. "I'm going to document every step. Both ways."

In math class, Mr. Janssen was talking about how his mortgage worked, how the bank charged interest on interest, and Theodore's hand shot up before he thought it through. "Can we test something? Simple versus compound, five years, same rate?"

Mr. Janssen smiled the way he did when a trap was about to spring. "Go ahead. Calculators out, people."

Theodore ran the simple version first. Fifty dollars the first year, fifty the second, fifty every year, because simple interest meant the money only ever grew on the original thousand. He wrote the total on the board: $1,250. Then Louane ran the compound version, where each year's interest joined the pile and earned interest of its own. Her final number came out bigger. Not by a fortune, but bigger, and it kept pulling ahead if you stretched the years out.

"Twenty years," Maddie called from the back row, already punching buttons. "Look at the gap now."

Theodore stood at the board, staring at the two numbers. So that was the catch, or maybe it wasn't a catch at all. His grandfather had told him the exact truth: one thousand two hundred fifty dollars, five years, simple. But there was a whole quiet machine in the world, ticking where nobody could see it, making money breed money.

That night he called his grandfather. "I'll take the deal," he said. "But I did the math, and I know what compound would do."

His grandfather laughed, a low rumble through the phone. "Then you learned more than most adults. Take the deal anyway, and when you're thirty, you tell me what the gap looks like."

Theodore hung up, found his notebook, and turned to a fresh page. Across the top he wrote: Year Six.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: To remove a tyre, a tyre lever is hooked under the tyre's edge and clipped to a spoke, then a second lever is used a little further along.
story:
The driving school parking lot was empty on Saturdays, which was why Mr. Demetriou let Leo and Cashton use it for their bike workshop. Leo's front tyre had gone flat on the ride over, and now it lay in a sad grey ring beside him while Cashton crouched nearby, eating the last of the cereal bars.

"You can't just pull it off with your fingers," Cashton said, watching Leo struggle. "I tried that once. My thumbs hurt for days."

Leo hooked his thumbs under the edge of the tyre and pulled until his knuckles went white. The rubber lifted a few millimetres and then snapped back down, like it was laughing at him. There had to be a reason bare hands failed, he thought, something about the way the edge sat down inside the rim where he couldn't see it. Last summer his dad had fixed a flat on the porch, and Leo remembered only fragments: his dad's hands moving quickly, small plastic things with hooks, a soft clicking sound. He hadn't paid attention. He'd been watching a beetle crawl across the step.

"Mr. Demetriou," Leo called across the lot. "Do you have those little plastic things for tyres? The hooked ones?"

"Tyre levers," Mr. Demetriou said, and tossed over a pair from the trunk of his beat-up teaching car. That was all he said. He went back to arranging his orange cones, leaving Leo with two flat plastic sticks and no instructions.

Leo slid the curved end of one lever under the tyre's edge. It caught, and the rubber lifted, but the moment he let go to reach for a better grip, it slipped off again. He stared at the lever, then at the spokes fanning out from the hub. There was a little notch near the other end of the lever. He pushed the notch onto the nearest spoke so it clipped in place, holding itself. Then he took the second lever and worked it in a little further along the edge. The tyre popped up over the rim like magic, or not magic, just a rule he had never known. With the tube out, he found the hole, patched it, and pumped the tyre until it was firm and coherent again, one solid round thing instead of a floppy mess.

Cashton contributed the last quarter of his cereal bar as payment, which Leo accepted even though it was mostly crumbs. They rode home together, Leo listening to his front wheel hum against the pavement, perfect and whole. At the corner where they split up, he thought about his dad on the porch, hands he should have watched more closely. Some things you only get taught once, and after that you have to teach yourself.

"Same time next Saturday?" Cashton called, already pedalling away.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
story:
Theodore had signed up to volunteer at the food bank that operated out of the back room of the animal shelter on Saturday mornings, mostly because Zahra had promised it would look good on their high school applications. He hadn't counted on the smell of kibble, or on the long line of people waiting outside with leashed dogs and empty tote bags.

"Grab a clipboard," Zahra said. "We sort people's orders before they come through. Mr. Chanthavong likes us to allocate the donated pet food evenly, so nobody at the end of the line gets nothing."

Mr. Chanthavong, who ran the shelter, pointed at the shelves. "We got thirty bags of dog food this week and nine of cat food. Cat owners always go home short." He said it like weather, a fact he'd stopped fighting.

Theodore started stacking, but a question nagged at him. If they always ran out of cat food, why did the whole line slow down near the middle? He watched through the doorway. A woman with a tabby cat in a carrier spent four minutes at the intake desk while a man with two dogs breezed through. Another cat carrier, another long pause. He couldn't see the cause directly, so he made a mental note like a neuron firing down a new path. Maybe the slowdown wasn't about food at all. Maybe people with cats had harder orders, because they needed the rarer items.

"Can I test something?" he asked Zahra. He pulled the cat food to the front of the sorting table and made a separate fast lane for cat orders, pre-bagging the portions. The next carrier came through in under a minute.

"Where did that idea come from?" Mr. Chanthavong asked.

"I watched the line. Cat people were the bottleneck." Theodore had expected to spend the morning being told what to do, and he'd been prepared to hate it. Instead he was rearranging the whole table like it was his.

While they restocked, an older volunteer asked, "Does anyone know how long food banks have even existed in Canada? I told my grandson it was something recent but he didn't believe me."

"1981," Theodore said. "The first one opened in Edmonton, Alberta. Zahra read it on the poster by the door and wouldn't stop quoting it all morning."

"I said it twice," Zahra said.

"Four times." He handed her a bag of cat kibble and grinned. "You want the explicit record kept straight, that's the price."

At noon the shelves were nearly bare, but every person in line had gone home with something, including the last woman, whose tabby meowed loudly from her carrier all the way to the parking lot.

fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
Jace stood at Gate 14 with his duffel bag between his feet, staring at the departures board even though he already knew his flight to Clearwater left at 4:55. He was going to the beach for a whole week, and he had not told anyone the truth: he could swim, but only in pools. The ocean scared him, because the ocean had rules he couldn't see.

Beside him, Wali was reading a travel brochure out loud. Wali wanted to win the airport's summer photo contest, and he kept arranging his backpack, his sunglasses, and even his snack crackers into shot after shot. "This one's called 'Traveler at Dawn,'" he said, squinting through his phone. "Be honest. Is it amazing or just pretty good?"

"It's pretty good," Jace said, but he wasn't really looking. Behind Wali, a life guard stand had been set up for some kind of beach safety display, complete with a poster of a red flag and a narrow band of blue arrows pointing away from the shore. A phrase on it caught his eye: rip current.

"Hey," Jace said. "What do you do if the water pulls you out?"

Wali lowered his phone. "My cousin says you swim sideways. Like this." He drew a line in the air with his finger, parallel to an imaginary beach. "You don't fight it straight back toward shore. You swim along the beach until you're out of the narrow part. Then the pull stops."

Jace turned that over. Swim sideways instead of against it. It sounded backwards, like giving up when you were being dragged away. But Wali's cousin was a life guard, and the poster agreed.

Then Jace noticed the moving walkway humming past their gate, packed with travelers gliding toward the far terminal. It was a current, he realized, a narrow one, with solid floor on both sides. He stepped on with Wali jogging alongside on the regular floor.

"Watch," Jace said. He tried walking straight back against the belt, and although his legs churned he barely moved, the walkway carrying him forward anyway. Then, instead of fighting it, he took two steps sideways, off the edge, and stood easily beside Wali on still ground.

"It works," Jace said. "You just go across, and you're out."

"It was logical," Wali agreed, and snapped a picture of Jace standing there, triumphant, with the walkway rushing past. "I'm calling this one 'The Escape.' Contest over."

Jace grinned and picked up his duffel. One week of ocean, and now he had one thing figured out. His boarding group was called, and he walked toward the jet bridge.

The lamp threw translucent curtains into a shadow on the wall, and she angled the screen so the light caught her face instead of her chin. Ten minutes later she looked at it again and hated it. Her smile was crooked and her eyes were half shut. She deleted it fast, before anyone could see, and went back to arguing with Lexi about which movie to watch.

The next morning, Kareem texted from the group chat: a screenshot of the deleted photo, complete with her caption naming Lexi's street and house number. Hailey's stomach dropped. She scrolled up and there it was, saved and shared, out of her hands entirely. She typed, then deleted, then typed again. "When did you even get that? I took it down after like ten minutes."

"Ten minutes was plenty," Kareem wrote back. "I saw it right away. Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

Hailey stared at the words. She had thought of deleting as undoing, like pulling a drawing off the fridge. Now she understood it was more like closing a door after people had already walked through it carrying pictures. She wanted to be sure, though, not just take his word. She asked Lexi to post a silly test photo of a sock puppet, delete it, and wait.

The next day Kareem sent the sock puppet screenshot too, plus one from a kid named Dev in the grade below, someone Hailey barely knew. A stranger, basically, holding a copy of something Lexi thought had vanished. Lexi deleted the whole thread and changed her settings, and Hailey did the same, turning off the location tags on her photos one by one like checking window locks.

"We're the antagonists of our own story if we post our address," Lexi said, and Hailey laughed even though her face still burned about the crooked smile. She made Lexi take a new photo, a good one, in the morning light with the curtains glowing, and captioned it with nothing but a single star. Before posting, she read it twice. Then she counted to ten, out loud, watching the caption, the picture, and her street name stay exactly where they belonged: nowhere at all. She put the phone facedown on the rug and said, "Your turn to pick the movie."

His legs felt like they were full of wet sand during Thursday's practice, and Noemy beat him down the court twice, which had never happened before. "You okay?" she asked, jogging beside him. "Fine," he said, and bricked the layup that followed. The playoff game against Riverside was Saturday. Three days.

He doubled down anyway. Friday morning he shot free throws until his arms shook, then stayed for sprints after school. That evening his neighbor, Mr. Marino, found him bouncing a ball off his garage door in the dark. "Big game?" Mr. Marino asked. "Saturday," Alexis said. "Riverside. He went inside without explaining, and Alexis stood there holding the ball, annoyed. That was vague. It wasn't even advice.

He thought about it anyway on the walk home. Kira trained maybe three days a week, spent Saturdays doing nothing much, and lately she thrived, quick off the dribble, always fresh in the fourth quarter. Alexis trained every single day and got slower. He turned the two facts over like coins. Maybe practice wasn't the thing itself. Maybe the getting-better part happened in between, in the rest, and he had been skipping the in-between for three straight weeks. It sounded wrong, almost lazy, but it fit what he was seeing better than anything else did. He tested it that night. No ball, no sprints. He ate dinner, stretched on the floor while his little brother called him the emperor of the couch, and went to bed early.

Saturday morning he felt something he hadn't felt in weeks. Light. In warmups his jump shot came off his hand smooth instead of heavy, and Noemy noticed. "You slept or something?" she asked. "Sort of," he said. "I did nothing on purpose."

The game was tight the whole way. With a minute left, Riverside led by one, and Alexis was still moving, still beating his man to every spot on the floor while the boys in yellow shorts bent over their knees. Kira grabbed the rebound and fired it ahead. Alexis took it in stride, two steps, and laid it high off the glass just as the buzzer started. The ball rolled around the rim, dropped through, and Noemy hit him at center court with both arms open.

story:
Quinn stood at the workbench in the barn with tweezers in one hand and a stopwatch in the other, glaring at a dish of seeds like it owed her money. "Bigger beaks win," she said for the third time. "Big beak, big seeds, big survivor. That's the whole formula." Kash, perched on a milk crate, shook his head. "Mr. Rahman's question didn't say that, though. It said explain what happened on those islands. Both directions."

Quinn dumped the seeds into a shallow pan and slid it across the bench. "Fine. We test it. You're the big beak." She handed him the heavy pliers. "I'm the small beak." She held up a pair of fine-tipped tweezers, which caught the light through the dusty window and looked almost translucent against her palm. "Big seeds, thirty seconds, grab as many as you can. Then small, soft ones. Ready?" They clicked the stopwatch and cracked sunflower seeds, and Kash beat her so badly on the big seeds that he did a small victory dance on the milk crate, which wobbled dangerously.

Then Quinn poured out a bowl of millet, tiny and soft, and they went again. Her tweezers flashed; his pliers fumbled, dropped, pinched empty air. She counted forty-one to his nine. Kash stared at his pliers as if they had betrayed him personally. "Okay," he admitted, "but real finches don't switch beaks. So what's the point?"

Before Quinn could answer, Loic came through the barn door waving his phone. "Message from Mr. Rahman. He couldn't come out today, so he sent the hint instead." He cleared his throat and read it aloud: "'To clarify your assignment: after the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds to Daphne Major, selection on the medium ground finches reversed, favouring smaller beaks. Think about what that tells you.'" Loic lowered the phone. "Reversed. Like a car in reverse."

Quinn looked at the millet, then at the pliers, then at the millet again. "The wet year made small seeds everywhere," she said slowly, picking up a pinch of millet and letting it sift through her fingers. "So the big beaks were standing in a whole island of millet. The little beaks, the ones that were losers before, suddenly they're me with the tweezers." She grabbed a marker from the bench and wrote on the back of Mr. Rahman's printed note: rain changes the seeds, the seeds change the winners, the winners pass on their beaks.

"So 'bigger is better' is wrong," Kash said. "It's bigger is better until it isn't." Quinn snorted. "It's better when the big seeds show up, which is most years, and then one rainy year flips the whole game." She bagged a scoop of millet and one sunflower seed to tape into their poster as evidence. "Mr. Rahman is going to love this." She held up the sunflower seed, pointed at Kash, and said, "You're the drought," then held up the millet and pointed at herself, "and I'm the rainy year of 1983."

"Five summers," he said when Forrest arrived with the cooler. "That's my savings plan. Every dollar we make today goes in the bank, and I want to know which account grows faster, simple interest or compound interest, over five years. Mr. Sadeghi says the answer isn't what people expect."

Forrest squinted at him. "You're doing math at a lemonade stand?"

"I'm doing research at a lemonade stand." Jayden spread his notebook on the table. On one page he had traced two lines, one creeping up like stairs, the other bending upward like a ramp getting steeper. The compound line pulled away from the simple line a little more each year, and money you couldn't see was doing it, quietly, year after year. He wanted to see the rule with his own numbers, so he'd worked the same starting amount both ways, five years each, and checked it twice.

Maelly biked up just as the first customer handed over a dollar. "Guess what I'm putting in my presentation," she said, parking the bike. "Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world."

Jayden's pencil stopped. "Wait. Did he, though? Where'd you read that?"

"My uncle said it. Everybody says it."

"Everybody saying a random quote isn't a source," Jayden said. "Check it first. That's the whole thing Mr. Sadeghi keeps hammering, verify before you quote." Maelly pulled out her phone and searched, thumbs flying. The lemonade sat untouched while she scrolled, and Jayden kept glancing over, because if she got up in front of the class and the quote was wrong, that would plague her whole presentation.

"Okay," Maelly said slowly. "It's everywhere, but every place just says 'attributed to Einstein.' Nobody has actual proof he said it. There's no reliable evidence at all."

"So drop the quote and lead with the math instead." Jayden slid his notebook toward her, tapping the two climbing lines. "Show them this. Simple interest, compound interest, five years, same start. Nobody even has to take Einstein's word for it."

Maelly grabbed the notebook and held it up to the light. "This is better than the quote."

"Forrest!" Jayden called to the curb, where Forrest was waving down a jogger with two sweating cups. "How many sales?"

"Six!"

Jayden wrote the number down, circled it, and poured the next round.

fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
story:
Easton pulled a box of oat cereal off the sorting table and turned it over, looking for damage. He had volunteered at the community garden's food bank shed for exactly forty minutes, and already he had a system: cans on the left shelf, dry goods in the middle, anything broken or open in the trash bin.

Ryan, who had been coming every Saturday since spring, snatched the box from him and tapped the small print near the top. "Toss it," he said. "See the date? It's one day past."

Easton looked. "Best if used by," he read aloud. "That's not an expiration date, is it?"

"It's a date," Ryan said, holding the box over the bin. "Dates mean old. Old means bad."

Easton didn't let go of the box. He was thinking about the milk in his own fridge at home, which his mom always sniffed and then poured on her cereal even when the printed date had come and gone. She said the date was the store's opinion, not a law. He had never checked whether that was true or just something she said.

"Wait," Easton said. "My mom says those dates are about quality, not safety. If the USDA says 'best if used by' shows when a food will be at its best quality, then it's not a food-safety date. It just means the cereal might be a little less crunchy."

Ryan lowered the box but kept his hand on it. "You're sure?"

"Not completely. But we can test it." Easton opened the inner bag, which was sealed and intact, poured a few flakes into his palm, and ate one. It tasted like oat cereal. A bit soft, maybe, but fine. He held out his palm to Ryan, who tried one too and shrugged.

Mr. Carvalho, who ran the shed and kept a laminated sheet of USDA guidelines taped inside the cabinet door, came over when he saw them hovering near the trash bin. He didn't lecture. He just flipped the cabinet open, tapped a paragraph, and let them read it for themselves. Easton skimmed down the page and grinned. Quality, not safety. Exactly what his mom had said, and now he knew it for real instead of just trusting her.

"So it goes on the shelf?" Ryan asked.

"It goes on the shelf," Mr. Carvalho said, "and you two are officially versatile. Yesterday you weeded beds, today you save cereal. I may have to make you ambassadors to the Saturday volunteers so they stop throwing out half the dry goods."

They stacked the cereal in the middle section, and Easton wrote a sticky note for the sorting table: CHECK THE SEAL, NOT JUST THE DATE. He wondered whether he would have spoken up if Ryan had been someone less friendly, maybe Robert from his math class, who argued about everything. Probably not, he decided. Probably he would have watched a perfectly good box go into the trash.

Ryan nudged him. "Next box, ambassador."

Easton reached into the crate and pulled out a jar of peanut butter, date and all.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
Charlotte had counted. On Tuesday, when Lionel's backpack zipper broke and his books spilled across the hallway, three people laughed and eleven people watched, and every one of the eleven pretended to be studying the bulletin board. On Thursday, when someone drew a cartoon of Lionel on the whiteboard before science, she counted again. Always watchers. Never just Lionel and whoever was being cruel.

"Is it always like this?" she asked Loick on Friday, splitting a sandwich on the bleachers behind the gym. "Like, is it ever just two people?"

Loick shrugged. He wanted the last half of the sandwich, she could tell, because he kept glancing at it while pretending not to. "Mr. Owusu has this old binder in his classroom," he said. "He keeps studies in it. There's one from 2001. They watched kids on school playgrounds and found other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes."

"Eighty-eight," Charlotte said.

"I didn't make it up." He took the sandwich half. "It's in the binder."

She thought about that number all through lunch. If other kids were almost always there, then the audience wasn't an accident. The audience was the weather the whole thing grew in. Which meant, maybe, that she wasn't a bystander at all. She was part of the 88 percent, whether she wanted to be or not.

Monday, someone took Lionel's chair in the lab and slid it to the far table, and the room went quiet in that listening way. Charlotte felt her face get hot, which was annoying, because she had a whole plan and the plan did not include blushing. She modified it on the spot. Instead of a speech, which would make everything bigger, she picked up the chair, carried it back, and said, "Lion, pass me the beaker, we're partners today." That was all. Small. Proportional, she thought, like the difference between a rain shower and a flood.

The room didn't explode. Two people went back to their worksheets. But Marcus, the chair thief, spent the rest of class kicking her stool leg, just lightly, just enough, and at recess he told everyone she and Lionel were "a thing now," and Lionel walked home alone anyway, faster than usual.

On Tuesday Charlotte caught up with him at the fence. "I'm not sorry I did it," she said, "but I'm sorry it landed on you."

Lionel considered this. "You could stop," he said.

"I could."

He pulled a folded paper from his pocket, the cartoon from the whiteboard, which he had apparently kept. "Or you could do it again tomorrow and look worse at it than yesterday," he said, and for the first time all week, he almost smiled. "Deal or truce?"

"Truce," said Charlotte, and they shook on it, which was ridiculous, and which neither of them took back.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
At 10:42 on Tuesday night, Ella's phone buzzed so many times it slid off her desk like a piston in a stuck engine, one jolt after another. The group chat, Tryouts Friday, had gone turbulent: forty messages in five minutes, mostly from Carissa, whose thumbs were flying.

"EMY-ROSE did you see the list?? 26 girls for 12 spots," Carissa wrote, followed by three sick-face emojis. "i've been sick to my stomach since lunch. can't eat. i hate this."

Emy-Rose answered a minute later. "same. my mom says it's just nerves. everyone gets nerves."

Ella stared at the screen. Her own stomach had been in knots since Monday, but Monday hadn't included any list. She scrolled back through the chat and noticed something: Carissa had been worrying since Saturday, five whole days before anyone would even step onto the gym floor. Nothing bad had actually happened yet. The buzzer hadn't sounded, no coach had cut anybody, nobody had missed a shot. The threat was still sitting in the future like a package nobody had opened.

She remembered a poster in the counsellor's hallway, the one she'd read while waiting for a flu shot in October. Fear, it said, is your body reacting to a threat happening right now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future. She'd walked past it a hundred times without thinking, but now the two words seemed to split Carissa's week into pieces. Saturday's dread hadn't been fear. Nothing was happening Saturday.

Ella decided to test it, quietly, in the chat. "Carissa," she typed, "what's the last time something bad actually happened to you, like for real, not might?"

A long pause, three dots appearing and vanishing. "um. fell off my bike in sept? why"

"And the tryout?" Ella wrote. "Has it happened?"

"no?? it's friday"

"So you've had five days of stress about zero minutes of actual tryout," Ella sent, then immediately worried she sounded like a poster herself. She added, "not saying it's not real. saying it's the might-happen kind. maybe that needs different coping than the happening kind."

Carissa replied with a single eye emoji, then: "ok that's weirdly helpful???" Emy-Rose sent "wait that actually makes sense" and a screenshot of a breathing app she'd found. For the next twenty minutes the three of them collaborated on a plan: Carissa would put her phone in the kitchen after nine o'clock, Emy-Rose would run drills with her at lunch instead of lying awake, and they'd all ride to the gym together Friday so nobody could spiral alone on the bus.

The plan worked, mostly. Carissa slept better Wednesday and Thursday, and she said the knots in her stomach loosened enough that she could eat her sandwich again. But on Friday, the moment the coach blew the whistle for the first sprint, Carissa's face went white and her legs shook so badly she false-started twice. Fear, the happening-now kind, was a different animal, and no group chat could train it away in advance. She didn't make the list of twelve. Ella did.

That night the chat was quiet for a long time. Then Carissa typed, "congrats ella. mean it." and, a minute later, "monday we're figuring out the on-the-court kind too." Ella looked at her name on the roster, then at Carissa's message glowing underneath it, and started typing back.

Meaning right now, this minute, while he stood at the counter pretending he had money.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers

fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
William had one objective for Saturday afternoon: find out where Jessy's surprise party was happening before it started at four. Payton had let the secret slip on Thursday, but then clammed up so completely that even begging got William nothing except a grin. So when Payton sent the group chat a photo captioned "getting ready," William stopped walking in the middle of the mall food court and stared at it. The picture showed balloons, a cake box, and a slice of Payton's own kitchen counter. No address, no street sign, nothing.

He sat down at a wobbly table beside a family sharing fries and opened the photo's info screen. He'd found it by accident last month while clearing space on his own phone, and since then he'd made a habit of checking. Payton, meanwhile, still used the same cracked phone he'd had since fifth grade and treated the settings menu like a foreign country he refused to visit.

There it was. Under the picture details, a small map with a pin sitting on it, and next to the map a line of numbers. William leaned closer. The pin wasn't on Payton's street, where he'd assumed the party would be. It was two neighbourhoods over, on Jessy's own street.

"You're grinning like you stole something," said a voice. Mr. Georgiou, his math teacher, stood holding a coffee, apparently also at the mall on a Saturday. William tilted the screen toward him before he could decide whether that was a good idea.

"See the map? Payton's phone did that," William said. "When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file. It's called EXIF metadata."

Mr. Georgiou took a slow inhale of his coffee steam. "And your friend posted that to a group chat with how many people?"

William's grin faded about halfway. "Fourteen." He hadn't thought about the fourteen. He'd thought about the party, about walking in at four o'clock and the look on Jessy's face. Now he was thinking about how Payton's phone, old enough that Payton called it obsolete at least once a week, had quietly told fourteen people exactly where Jessy lived, to the pinpoint, because nobody had ever told them it was doing that.

He typed a warning to Payton instead of a reply, then deleted it and typed again. "Cool pic. Check your photo details. Seriously." He pressed send, and the message sat there with a single grey checkmark. Fourteen people had the pin. He couldn't unsend the photo, couldn't unsee the coordinates, and there was no way to know who else had already tapped the map.

William stood, wove past the family with the fries, and headed for the bus that went to Jessy's street. He would arrive early, knock on the door, and tell them in person to turn location services off before anyone took another picture. It would probably ruin the surprise for him completely, being there three hours ahead of the balloon gang, sitting on Jessy's porch steps while Payton's phone kept glowing in his pocket with messages he didn't open. Jessy's mother pulled into the driveway at three fifteen, saw him, and waved with the confused half-smile of someone trying to remember if she'd invited him.

"Jessy's not home yet," she called through the car window. "You want to wait inside?"

"Somebody's coming at four," William said. "We should talk before they get here."
