story:
The binder on Grandpa's desk was older than Jayden's dad, and it held five years of bank statements. Jayden had come to the house for one reason: the ad from the bike shop said the new Trailblazer 300 cost two hundred forty dollars, and his savings account had exactly two hundred ten in it, plus whatever interest had piled up while he ignored it. He figured five years of interest had to be plenty.

He spread the statements across the kitchen table. Grandpa slid a mug of hot chocolate beside him and said nothing, which was his way of saying get on with it. Jayden wrote the balance from each year on a napkin, then wrote it again beside the first column. In one column the interest sat there like a lazy cat, the same flat amount every year. In the other, each year's interest earned interest of its own. "Compound," Jayden said out loud. "That's the good one." He added it up twice, because the first total made him want to add it a third time. His account would hold two hundred thirty-one dollars. He shot a text to Lachlan: BIKE IS MINE. DEAL WITH IT.

Then he found the bike binder. Grandpa had kept ads from the same shop going back years, which was either bizarre or genius, and Jayden decided genius, because there was the Trailblazer, the same bike, priced every single year. His eye went down the column and his stomach dropped somewhere near his sneakers. The price had climbed faster than his balance. Every year. Without a single exception.

He read it again, slower. His account grew. The price grew faster. So even though the number in his account got bigger every year, it bought less of that bike every year. His two hundred ten used to cover most of it, and his two hundred thirty-one now covered less. It was like watching a race where both runners moved forward and the gap got wider anyway. "My brain is doing something weird," he muttered. "Some neuron in there just flipped over."

He dreaded texting Lachlan back, but he did it anyway: NEVER MIND. MATH BETRAYED ME. The reply came fast: HA. Malek added a row of laughing faces. Jayden slapped the table, and Grandpa looked up from his crossword.

"Problem?"

"The money grew and the bike got farther away at the same time. That should be illegal." Jayden held up the two napkin columns. "I need a savings account whose interest outruns the price of things. That's the whole game, isn't it?"

Grandpa set down his pencil, walked to the fridge, and pinned the oldest bike ad next to the newest one. "Now you're asking the right question. What are you going to do about it?"

Jayden looked at the two prices hanging there like a before-and-after picture, grabbed a fresh napkin, and started a third column.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Xavier balanced the display board against the wall of the community centre gym and frowned at his caption. Two weeks of work on the northern communities project, and one line was bugging him: "Elder Qitsualik, an Inuit, describes hunting on the sea ice." Something about it felt off, though he could not have said why.

"You're still staring at that?" Felix said, lugging a box of poster paint toward the storage room. "It's one caption. Nobody reads captions anyway." He rattled the door handle, then pointed at the sign taped above it. "Keep this stuff away from the stage curtains, by the way. It says flammable right on the box." Felix had argued the whole ride over that the display was fine as it was, and Xavier was starting to wonder if he was the only one who cared.

But the wondering was the problem. Xavier turned the sentence over in his head the way he did with a math proof, looking for the hidden rule he was missing. The word Inuit named a whole people, so was it like saying "a French" instead of "a French person"? If that was the pattern, then there ought to be a singular word, the way one die was part of many dice. He had a simple way to test it, too: ask someone who would actually know instead of guessing.

Lyra was taping up her family's photos by the stage, part of the centre's heritage wall where everyone had pinned a note saying where their families came from. Xavier waited until she finished adjusting the crooked frame of a picture of her grandmother in a embroidered parka.

"Can I ask you something for my caption?" he said. "I wrote 'an Inuit,' and it feels wrong."

Lyra smiled like he had passed a small test. "Inuit means 'the people' in Inuktitut," she said. "One person is an Inuk. My grandmother would say she's an Inuk."

That was it. The hidden rule had a name for the singular, exactly as his pattern had predicted, and now he could fix the line. Xavier went back to his board, pulled the caption off its Velcro backing, and printed a new one, checking twice that he had it right: Elder Qitsualik, an Inuk, describes hunting on the sea ice. Each caption was a component of the whole display, he had realized on the drive over, and a wrong word in one piece made every other piece look shaky.

Felix wandered over, read the new line, and was quiet for a moment. "Okay," he said, "I take it back. People do read captions." He picked up the tape and held out the roll. "So what's an Inuk man doing on a poster about sea ice? Tell me the whole thing."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
story:
The lights went out just as Austin was about to microwave popcorn, and he let out a groan that could probably be heard three houses down. His friend Dawson was already in the backyard with the telescope, because tonight was the one night Mr. Do had promised them a clear view of Saturn, and now the whole street had gone dark and gleaming with stars. That was the good news. The bad news was that Austin was starving, and the fridge was the only interesting thing left indoors.

He opened the fridge door, and its little internal light did not come on, which somehow made the whole thing creepier. He peered into the opaque containers on the middle shelf, decided he could not classify any of them as an actual snack, and shut the door. Two minutes later he opened it again. Then again, hunting for the string cheese he was almost sure existed. Each time, cold air rolled out over his feet like something the fridge could not afford to lose.

"Stop opening it!" Dawson yelled from the yard. "Aryan looked it up on his phone. It says a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as the door stays closed. You keep standing there letting the cold out."

"Four hours?" Austin shouted back. "That's it?"

"That's it. So decide what you want first, then open it exactly once."

Austin stood in the dark kitchen and changed his mind about the string cheese hunt. One trip, one grab, like a space mission. He planned it: leftovers on the bottom shelf, apples in the drawer, and the cheese, if it was real, behind the milk. He opened the door once, swept the shelf with his hand, and came out with an apple, two cheese sticks, and, by accident, a jar of pickles he refused to put back even though it wrecked his plan.

In the backyard, Aryan had dragged the telescope into position and was holding his phone upside down over a star chart. Mr. Do leaned over the fence in his bathrobe, pointing at a bright dot low in the sky. "There she is," he said. "Ringed and beautiful."

"Okay, this is amazing," Austin said, handing out the cheese sticks like prizes. "Saturn plus snacks plus no lights anywhere. Should we do a vote on who spots the moon first?"

"Obviously," Dawson said. "It's a democracy out here now."

Aryan won the moon vote hunt and did a victory lap around the lawn. Austin bit into his apple, looked up at Saturn, and decided power cuts were maybe the best thing that had ever happened, at least until the lights flickered back on and Aryan yelled, "Everyone freeze, don't move, the dark was better!"

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
Mila had until six o'clock to devise a pasta sauce from scratch, because her grandmother was coming for dinner and had announced, over the phone, that jar sauce tasted like "sad tomatoes." So Mila took her allowance to the farmers' market on Saturday morning and bought a bag of onions, a bunch of basil, and two baskets of tomatoes so ripe they smelled like summer even through the paper bag.

At the knife-sharpening stall, Mr. Foster, who ran the honey booth next to it, watched her eye the onions. "You planning to cry your way through those?" he asked.

"I don't know how to cut one," Mila said. "Last time I ended up with chunks the size of dice and a Band-Aid on my thumb."

He walked her through the claw grip. Curl your fingertips under so your knuckles guide the blade, and the edge can't reach your fingertips. Mila practiced on an onion right there on the stall's cutting board, her fingers tucked like a small pink crab, and the knife ticked against her knuckles instead of her skin. It felt awkward for exactly one onion, and then it didn't.

Gurshan and Wassim showed up at noon, partly to help and partly because Wassim had heard there was a stall selling lemonade. They carried Mila's bags back to her kitchen, and she set them to washing tomatoes while she chopped. The sauce went together in her big pot: onion first, then tomatoes crushed by hand, basil torn in at the end because Gurshan insisted tearing was more spontaneous than cutting and Mila was too busy stirring to argue.

By five thirty she had a real sauce, thin and watery but fragrant, and pasta bubbling in the next pot. Wassim, assigned to drain the noodles, lifted the whole pot toward the sink.

"Wait," Gurshan said, grabbing a mug from the counter. "Give me a cup of that first."

"The pasta water? It's all cloudy."

"That's the point," Gurshan said. "Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta."

Mila had assumed the cloudiness meant the water was dirty, not useful. She poured half the mug into her thin sauce and stirred. Within a minute the sauce stopped sliding off the spoon and started coating it. She kept stirring and watched it cling, then added the drained pasta straight into the pot and tossed everything together.

Her grandmother arrived at six, tasted one forkful, and said nothing for a full ten seconds. Then she pointed her fork at the bowl. "You made this today? All of it?"

"Me, Gurshan, and Wassim," Mila said. "And Mr. Foster taught me not to cut my fingers off."

Her grandmother took a second helping, and Wassim put the mug of leftover pasta water in the fridge, labeled with tape: "SAUCE MAGIC."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
story:
Grayson was at his grandpa's house, lying on the braided rug with his phone held above his face, when the group chat turned mean. Someone had posted a picture of Fionn's science project, a lopsided model of the equator made from a hula hoop and clay, and the comments rolled in fast. "Looks like a donut." "Fionn can't even do a circle." Grayson laughed at the first one before he caught himself, because the hula hoop did look like a donut, but by the third comment his stomach felt tight.

He typed "guys chill" and then deleted it. He knew from experience how that would go. Last month Owen had said something similar in another chat, and the whole thing had gotten worse, sharper, more joking on the surface and less joking underneath. Grayson scrolled up to reread the donut comment, and it was gone. Deleted. Then the next one vanished too, right before his eyes, like someone sweeping footprints off a beach.

He sat up so abruptly that the old cat, who had been asleep on his sneakers, bolted off the porch in outrage. "Sorry, Biscuit," Grayson called, but his mind was somewhere else. He began to assume something and then stopped and tested it instead. The messages could be deleted, but only by whoever sent them. What if he captured them before they disappeared? He took a screenshot of the two comments still standing, his thumb hovering, and when a third mean one appeared he grabbed that too. The screen made its little camera click, and Grandpa looked over from his crossword.

"You photographing my cat again?"

"Worse," Grayson said. "Group chat." He explained the whole thing while Grandpa poured lemonade that smelled like summer and sounded like wind chimes when the ice shifted. Grandpa sipped and nodded. "You can't unring a bell, but you can write down what it sounded like," he said, which was not helpful, actually, but sounded wise.

That evening Grayson composed a message to Mr. Karimi, their homeroom teacher, and reread it three times before sending.

Hi Mr. Karimi. Some people in our class chat were making fun of Fionn's project. They deleted the messages, but I took screenshots before they could, so there's still a record if that helps. I didn't want to just yell at everyone because last time that made it worse. What should I do?

Mr. Karimi replied within the hour: Thank you, Grayson. This helps more than you know. Screenshots like these let me act on something instead of just hearing "trust me, it happened." Leave the rest to me for now.

The next morning Fionn found Grayson at his locker. "Karimi talked to them. All of them. Individually. It was like watching a row of sunflowers droop." Fionn grinned and knocked his shoulder against Grayson's. "So did you save my donut picture at least? Because honestly, it did look like a donut."

"Two donuts," Grayson said. "I assume that's why you glued the extra clay on top."

Fionn held up the hula hoop, which he had apparently brought to school for reasons known only to Fionn, and spun it on one finger like a circus performer. "Sprinkles."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important.
story:
Florence sat in the back row of the computer lab at Camp Birchwood, staring at a screen full of angle brackets. She had signed up for the web design workshop because her brother told her it would be easy, and she hated that he had been wrong. The instructor, Ms. Georgiou, had shown them how to make a heading with tags, but Florence's page still looked like a pile of broken furniture.

"What's yours about?" asked Alaric, leaning over from the next computer. His page already had a green background and a picture of a frog.

"A guide to the camp's best canoe routes," Florence said. "Except right now it's a guide to nothing, because I can't even get the title to look right."

She had typed her title between two tags she'd found in an old handout, but it came out small and cramped, sitting meekly in the corner like an apology. She tried making the font bigger, letter by letter, and it still looked wrong. Ms. Georgiou walked past and said only, "Think about importance," which annoyed Florence because it wasn't an answer, it was a riddle.

At lunch she picked at her pasta and thought about last summer, when she'd quit the swim team after two weeks because the older girls intimidated her and she'd told everyone she was bored instead. She still wasn't sure that had been a lie. She remembered deciding that the deep end was for other people, and she wondered whether she was doing the same thing now, deciding that code was for people like Alaric, who seemed to understand it the way some kids understood the rules of a game they'd played since they were five.

Back in the lab, she opened the handout again and read it properly this time, all the way down instead of skimming. There it was: HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important. She had been using h4, somewhere in the middle, for the biggest thing on her page. She typed h1 instead, closed the tag, and the title jumped out big and bold across the screen. She tried h6 on a small note at the bottom and watched it shrink, confirming the pattern: the number worked backwards from what she'd assumed.

"Wait, that's it?" Alaric said, looking over. "The smaller number is the bigger heading?"

"Six levels, and h1 is the most important," Florence said, feeling defiant and pleased at once, like she'd found the deep end wasn't so deep after all.

Then she added one more line, and the title slid to the centre of the page. "There," she said, and turned the screen toward Jamie, who had just wandered over with a popsicle. "That's the front door. Now people will actually want to come in."

Jamie leaned down and read the title out loud. "Best Canoe Routes at Birchwood, by Florence."

"By Florence," she agreed, and hit save.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Either person on a date can say no to holding hands, a hug or a kiss at any time, and a respectful partner accepts that answer without pressure.
story:
The bleachers were loud by the time Livia found her seat, which was good, because it meant nobody could hear her heart going like a drumline. Aliza waved from the third row and moved her jacket off the spot she'd saved. That was the whole plan: watch the game, split a pretzel, walk home after. Livia's mom had called it a date, out loud, twice, which was mortifying, but it was also true.

Before kickoff, Aliza's hand landed on top of Livia's on the metal bench. Livia looked at it. A test, she thought. Not a test of whether she liked Aliza, because she did. A test of whether she could say a word that felt like breaking something.

"No," Livia said. "Not that."

Aliza took her hand back like it was nothing, like returning a borrowed pencil. "Okay." Then she pointed at the field. "Look, they appointed a seventh grader as captain. Number twelve. He's tiny."

Livia exhaled. She had a whole theory, worked out last week, and the first part of it had just held up. Her older cousin Rosa had told her a story once, about a boy who asked twice, who slid his arm around again after she'd moved it away, and Rosa had laughed like it was normal. Livia had decided that was a pattern, not a rule. A pattern meant something somebody made up. A rule had to run both ways, like the offside rule, no exceptions for either team.

She tested the second part at the pretzel stand. Ms. Aquino, who ran the concession booth for every home game, handed over the change and said, "Big crowd tonight. Proportional to how badly we beat them last year, I'd say." Livia laughed, and when Aliza offered her the last half of the pretzel, Livia said, "No, it's yours," and Aliza just ate it. No pressing. No "come on, just take it."

In the fourth quarter the home team fumbled twice, and Aliza groaned and hid her face in her scarf, and Livia found she liked watching her more than the game. Through the whole second half she kept one idea in front of her like a lens: if Aliza could take a no, then Livia could give one, and give it honestly, without softening it into a joke.

The buzzer went off and everyone spilled down the bleachers toward the gate. The crowd thinned out on the sidewalk. At the corner where their streets split, Aliza opened her arms for a hug.

Livia stepped back. "Not today."

Aliza dropped her arms and smiled. "Okay. See you Monday?"

"Monday," Livia said, and turned down her street, her heart still drumming, but lighter now.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A round-robin, in which each person speaks in turn around the circle, gives quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas.
story:
Alexandra spread the papers across the kitchen table and set a plate of crackers beside them so nobody could accuse her of running a club without snacks. On Saturday the Nature Club would meet in her garage, and she was in charge for the first time. She had an agenda, printed in careful block letters, but last month's meeting kept replaying in her head: Aubree talking for ten straight minutes about the bake sale, Omar arguing back, and two other members leaving before the end without saying a single word. One of them was a boy named Daniel who kept a notebook full of bird drawings and never opened it at meetings.

"It's like a wall," Omar said when she described it to him on Friday after school. "Aubree talks, everyone else waits, and then the meeting's over."

"Then they need a rule," Alexandra said. "A rule that makes people wait for each other."

At the meeting on Saturday, Aubree arrived with a poster about the bake sale income, which she wanted to distribute across three different club projects. She pinned it up before anyone sat down. Alexandra slid the crackers toward her and said, "First we go around the circle. It's called a round-robin. Each person speaks in turn, and nobody talks twice until everyone's talked once."

Aubree opened her mouth. Alexandra pointed at Omar, who sat at the far end. Omar suggested a cleanup day at the creek. The next member, a quiet girl, said they should sell seed packets. Then it was Daniel's turn, and the garage went so silent that Alexandra could hear a wasp tapping the window.

Daniel opened his notebook. "The creek has a heron nest," he said. "If we clean up on the north bank, we'll scare them off. But the south bank is where all the trash is anyway, because it catches everything the current drops there. If we do that side, we clean more and the nest stays safe."

Aubree stared at the poster she could no longer mention yet, her marker going brittle and dry in her fist as she gripped it. When the round came back to her, she said, "Fine. South bank. And Daniel picks where the seed money goes." Daniel turned pink and wrote something in his notebook.

Afterward, Alexandra collected the agenda papers, which had somehow become placemats crusted with cracker crumbs. Aubree lingered by the door. "Same system next time?" she asked. "Even if I have a poster?"

"Especially if you have a poster," Alexandra said, and Aubree laughed so hard she knocked the wasp cup off the shelf.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Bentley had never missed a home game all season, and he wasn't about to start tonight, even with his science worksheet folded in his back pocket. The worksheet had a question about how long a monarch larva takes to become a butterfly, and he figured he could think about it at halftime. For now he sat two rows behind the bench with Nathaniel and Malak, watching the scoreboard tick through a game that meant everything. If the Falcons won, they would finish second in the league standings. If they lost, they would drop to third.

"Second place," Malak said, ticking the numbers on his fingers. "That's pretty good, right?" Bentley nodded, but something bothered him. He had looked at the standings that morning, and the Falcons and the fourth-place team were separated by exactly one win, the same gap that separated the Falcons from first. Second and fourth sounded miles apart, and first and second sounded like a rivalry, but the actual distance was identical. One win, one loss, either way.

In the third quarter the Falcons fell behind by nine, and Bentley stopped thinking about standings at all. He watched their point guard, a kid everyone called Juice, push the ball up the floor again and again. The shooting percentage on the scoreboard said the Falcons were at thirty-eight percent for the game, a number that compressed every shot, good and bad, into one figure. "That number doesn't tell you he made the last four," Bentley said to Nathaniel, nodding at Juice. "The percentage catches up slower than the game does."

The comeback couldn't sustain itself forever. The Falcons clawed back to within two, then within one, and with eleven seconds left Juice drove the lane and banked in a shot that put them ahead. The gym went so loud that Bentley felt it in his teeth. When the buzzer finally sounded, the Falcons had won by two, and second place was theirs.

Afterward, in the lobby, Malak bought a program with the final standings printed inside. "Look at this," he said, tapping the page. "We're second and Riverside's first, and it just says one, two. It doesn't say how far apart they are." Bentley grinned, because he'd figured out the same thing that morning. "A ranking shows the order but not the distance," he said. "First and second could be a hundredth apart or a mile apart. You have to go look." He pulled out his crumpled worksheet, and there on the back he had written the two teams' records side by side, proof that the gap was exactly one win. Then he paused, laughed, and held it up. "Also, I still have to write a paragraph about a larva by Monday, and it's your fault it's late, Nathaniel. You kept feeding me nachos."

"Nachos build champions," Nathaniel said, and held out the tray.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
Matteo set his pencil down and stared at the page until the numbers seemed to wobble. Three homework problems sat finished in his notebook, and every one had come out wrong according to the answers in the back of the book. The teacher had said it again and again: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Matteo could hear Mr. Morin's voice saying it, patient and almost cheerful, but somehow his pencil only remembered half the time.

The kitchen smelled of onions browning in the pan, and his grandmother hummed at the stove while rain ticked against the window. He copied the first problem onto a fresh sheet: x + 7 = 19. Last night he had subtracted seven and somehow written twelve, as if the seven had drifted over to the wrong side like a sneaky houseguest. He drew a line straight down through the equals sign, splitting the page into two halves, and tried imagining the equation as a seesaw. If he took seven off one side, what happened to the other if he took nothing?

"Nonna," he said, tapping the sign, "who decided this should be two little lines? Why not a squiggle, or a dot, or something fancier?"

She came over, wiping her hands on her apron, and squinted at his notebook. "Robert Recorde," she said. "A Welshman. 1557. He said no two things could be more equal than two parallel lines, so that's what he drew." She tapped the page once, vigorous as a judge. "Before him, people just wrote words."

Matteo looked at the two short lines. Two things, perfectly equal, exactly the same distance apart all the way along. He despised getting answers wrong, but this he liked: someone, almost five hundred years ago, had looked at this shape and thought, that is what equal means. If the lines were truly equal, then whatever happened on one side had to happen on the other, or the lines would be lying.

He tried again. x + 7 = 19. He wrote minus seven under the left side, then minus seven under the right side, keeping the two halves balanced like twin pans on a scale. Nineteen minus seven was twelve, so x was twelve. He checked by adding back: twelve plus seven, nineteen. The answer in the book matched. On the next problem, 4x = 32, he divided both sides by four and got eight, and on the third he subtracted first, then divided, both sides every time, like feeding two identical dogs at once.

He texted Isabel a photo of the page with the vertical lines drawn through every equation, and her reply came back in seconds: "why the prison bars?" He started typing an answer, then stopped, wondering how to explain two parallel lines in a message. Outside, the rain picked up, drumming hard against the glass.

"They're not bars," he said out loud to the empty kitchen. "They're a promise."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Alicia wanted one thing before the school talent show on Friday: for nobody to see the dance blog she'd written in fifth grade. She'd found it again by accident, when Chris typed her name into a search during computer lab. "Look, it still exists," he said, pointing at the screen. "I deleted that two years ago," Alicia said. The page loaded anyway, with the photos she'd posted of herself in the backyard, in a leotard, mid-cartwheel. Beside each photo, the old posts described exactly where she practiced, right down to the corner of Elm Street.

She tried to isolate where the copy was coming from. The URL wasn't her blog's address anymore; it belonged to some other site. She clicked around and found a banner with strange orange lettering. "What's a Wayback Machine?" Walker asked, leaning over from the next computer. Mr. Lim passed behind them on his rounds, but he only paused, read the screen, and moved on. Alicia scrolled to the bottom of the page and found her answer written in small print. Since 1996 the Internet Archive had been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone could look at old versions of many websites there. Her blog had been public once, and someone had saved it, and the whole world could still read it.

"That's a plague," Walker said. "Like, a permanent plague of embarrassing fifth graders." Alicia barely heard him. She was thinking about the photos. If the blog still existed, then the street name still existed too, and her practice schedule, and the shot of her house with the number on the door visible. Strangers she'd never met could see all of it, and she'd never know who had. The thought made the back of her neck hot.

There was one thing she could test. She found the archive's contact page and a form for asking that a page be removed. It asked a lot of questions, and she filled in every box she could, then emailed the link to her mom from her school account. "Will they take it down?" Chris asked. "I don't know yet," Alicia said. "But it can't hurt to ask." She refreshed the page once, twice, watching her fifth-grade self hang upside down in the cartwheel photo, arms out, eyes squeezed shut.

Thursday afternoon, she checked again before rehearsal. The page loaded partway, then stopped at a gray notice where her blog used to be. Alicia read it twice, then looked up. "It's gone," she said. "It's really gone." Walker leaned over, squinting at the empty gray box. "So what do we do about that video of me falling off the stage last year?"

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The lights died at 7:14, because that was the exact moment Marcus's microwave clock went dark along with his popcorn, and he was the kind of kid who noticed things like that. He stood in the sudden black of the kitchen, listening. The refrigerator had stopped humming. The hallway light under the apartment door had vanished too. That was his first clue. If it were just his apartment, the breaker in the hall closet would have popped, but the hallway belonged to the building, not to his family, so whatever had killed his microwave had killed the whole floor. Maybe the whole building.

"Power cut," his grandmother announced from the living room, in the tone of someone reporting rain. He heard her shuffling toward the kitchen, then the scrape of a drawer, then the clink of a matchbox. Marcus's stomach did a small flip. In the dark, with her hands searching along a countertop crowded with mail and yesterday's newspaper, a candle flame could touch anything.

"Wait, hold on." He felt his way along the wall, bumped the table with his hip, and found the third drawer down, the one that held batteries, rubber bands, and two flashlights nobody had touched since the last storm. He clicked one on and a beam of yellow light swung across the room, catching his grandmother mid-match-strike, the little flame trembling above her thumb.

"Safety agencies say to use flashlights instead of candles in a power cut, Gran. A candle can easily start a fire in a dark house." He held the flashlight out like a prize on a game show. "Fire-safety unit, sixth grade. Mr. Johansson made us chant it."

His grandmother snorted, but she shook the match out and took the flashlight. "Chanting teachers. Fine, you win this round." She patted his shoulder on her way past. "Go check on the neighbors, since you're so clever."

Marcus knocked on Ayden's door first. Ayden answered holding his phone with the flashlight app on, screen so dim it made him look lethargic, like a boy powered by two dying batteries. "Six percent," Ayden said mournfully. "My phone is losing the will to live." Marcus lent him the second flashlight and they climbed the stairs together to the fourth floor, where Hayley had set up shop at the stairwell window, selling glow sticks from her camping supply at a quarter each, announcing to anyone who passed that she was a serious entrepreneur and this was her founding night. Business was slow. The dark building was full of phone lights.

Back downstairs, Marcus stood at his window and looked out. The streetlights on their block were dead, but three streets over, the whole row glowed orange and ordinary. So the cut had edges, which meant crews could find those edges, which meant the lights would probably come back. Probably. His grandmother called from the kitchen, asking if the flashlight could convey enough light for her to finish the crossword, or whether she had to wait for the ceiling to solve the last four across clues. Marcus raised the beam toward her voice and said, "Six letters, starts with F, means the opposite of lazy."

"Ha," she said, and tapped her pencil twice. "Lethargic?"

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
story:
Colton had one hundred and eighty-two dollars in his savings account, and the bank teller had just told him something that made no sense at all. "Your statement shows both," she said, sliding the paper under the glass. "Simple and compound. Same rate, different results."

He sat down on the bench near the windows to stare at the numbers. He was saving for a laptop before he graduated, four years away, and he needed to know which kind of interest would actually get him there. Simple interest, as far as he could tell from the statement, added the same flat amount every year, like stacking identical bricks. Compound interest added interest on the interest already earned, and the statement's graph climbed a little more steeply each year. But a graph was not a promise. He wanted to see the actual number at the end.

Viktor plopped down beside him, holding a lollipop the teller had given him even though they were both fourteen. "You look like you're doing math in a bank, which is illegal."

"I'm trying to figure out what my money does in five years," Colton said. "Compound, once a year." He pulled out his calculator. His deposit was 182 dollars, and the yearly rate was 3 percent, which he wrote as 0.03. He tried 182 times 1.03 and got 187.46, which was one year. Then he started multiplying by 1.03 again, and again, losing his place twice.

"You know there's a power key," Viktor said, pointing at the little button with a small raised box on it. "My sister showed me. It does the multiplying for you."

Colton's thumb hovered over it. He typed 182, then the power key, then 5, and hit equals. The screen showed 211.01. He checked it against his slow version, where he'd only gotten through three years, and the three-year numbers matched exactly. So with interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years was the starting amount times 1.03 to the power of n. He tried it with n as 4 for his graduation year, then n as 5 anyway, just to see the far edge of it.

"Two hundred eleven dollars," he said. "In five years."

"So you're rich," said Viktor.

"So I'm short. The laptop is four hundred." Colton drummed his fingers on the statement, thinking about the arid stretch of months ahead where he'd have nothing to add, then about the birthday money in March, and the twenty dollars a month he could skim if he stopped buying soda at lunch. He could deposit extra, and that deposit would compound too. He pulled the deposit slip toward him and started writing.

"What's that for?" Viktor asked, crumpling his lollipop stick.

"Every dollar I donate to my future self," Colton said, standing up and getting in line behind a woman filling out forms for some kind of amendment to her mortgage. He held up the slip so Viktor could read it. "First payment, today."

"Hey," Viktor called after him, digging in his pocket. "Wait for me, I've got a five."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Putting a little air in a new tube before fitting it gives it shape, so it is less likely to twist or get pinched under the tyre.
story:
Anthony pushed his bicycle through the door of the dilapidated laundromat, its front tyre flopping against the wheel rim with every step. Gabriel was already there, guarding two duffel bags of clothes while the dryers thundered, and he looked up when the tyre made its sad, flat slap against the tiles.

"Flat again?" Gabriel asked. "That's the second one this month."

The last one had happened on the bridge over the canal, and Anthony still remembered pushing his bike home in the drizzle, passing the pizza place he couldn't stop at because his shoes were soaked through. He had promised himself then that he would learn to fix it himself instead of waiting for his uncle to visit with his toolbox. Now he had the toolbox part: tyre levers, a patch kit, a spare tube, and a small pump, all zipped into a pouch he'd spent his allowance on.

He flipped the bike upside down on the folding table beside the dryers and loosened the wheel. The levers popped the tyre off its edge easily enough, but when he tried to feed the new tube in, it kept folding and twisting. He would work one section under the tyre, turn to the next, and find that the rubber had bunched up somewhere behind him, pinched between the tyre and the rim.

Gabriel leaned over. "Maybe you're putting it on wrong."

"I'm putting it on the same way every time," Anthony said. "That's the problem. I can't tell what I'm changing." He had learned in science class that when you test something, you change one variable at a time, otherwise you can't tell what made the difference. So far he had only one observation: the floppy tube got caught, every time.

He stared at the limp circle of rubber in his hands. A tube with no shape went anywhere the tyre pushed it. What if he gave it some shape first? He pressed the pump head onto the valve and adjusted the fitting until it gripped, then gave a few careful strokes. The tube rounded out into a fat, soft loop, like a skinny doughnut. When he laid it into the rim this time, it sat where he placed it, and the tyre slid back over it without pinching anything. He pumped it firm, and the tyre stood up round and solid.

"Nice," Gabriel said, hauling the first duffel bag off the table. He lugged it toward the dryers, then paused. "Hey, Mr. Kaya said you could use his garage pump, by the way. He's outside waiting to tell you. Says he saw you coming with the flat."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and old potato chips, which was why Nicholas's mom called it his "lab." He had taped a giant periodic table poster to the wall between the rake and a shelf of rusty coffee cans, and he glared at it like it had insulted his family. Monday's quiz would ask him to find the number of protons in any element, and right now the whole chart looked like a crossword designed by someone with a grudge.

Kyleigh sat on an overturned bucket, kicking her sneakers against a hubcap. "You could just memorize it," she said.

"I tried. It fell out of my head by dinner." Nicholas tapped the poster. "There has to be logic in here somewhere. Everything in science has a pattern, even if you can't see it."

Hunter, sprawled across an old lawn chair, held up a flashlight. "I'm the lighting crew. Also, I found this behind your dad's workbench." He tossed over a crumpled science museum brochure. Nicholas smoothed it flat on the workbench. There was a timeline inside, and one photo stopped him: a messy handwritten chart with lots of empty squares.

"Dmitri Mendeleev," Kyleigh read over his shoulder. "It says he published an early version of the periodic table in 1869. Look how few elements he had. There are gaps all over it."

"He left blanks?" Nicholas leaned closer. He ran his finger across the top of his own poster until he found the little number in each box, the atomic number, right there above every symbol. Carbon, 6. Oxygen, 8. Gold, 79. He grabbed a marker and wrote on a scrap of sandpaper: the atomic number equals the number of protons. It was so obvious it was almost annoying.

"So to find protons, I just read the number," he said. "That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"Test it," Hunter said, grinning. "Quiz me. Wait, no, quiz yourself, I don't want to learn anything on a Saturday."

Nicholas drilled until his voice went hoarse, salvaging a bag of stale pretzels from the shelf as a prize for every ten correct. Hunter's laughter was infectious; even the flashlight wobbled when he doubled over. By dusk, Nicholas could answer anything. Potassium, 19. Copper, 29. Neon, 10.

He flopped back into the lawn chair, victorious. "Mendeleev would be proud. Guy writes one chart in 1869 and now I can't fail Monday."

Kyleigh pulled the brochure from under the pretzel bag and squinted at it. "Nicholas? It says here his table wasn't even the first try. Somebody else proposed one earlier and it got ignored."

Hunter clicked the flashlight off and on. "So Monday's quiz could have been on the other guy's chart?"

Nicholas sat up very slowly and reached for the marker again.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Austin pressed his left index finger down on the high E string for the third time, and the pain shot up like a spark. He winced, shook his hand, and set the guitar flat across his lap.

"Still hurting?" Raylan asked from the next chair in Ms. Yoon's music classroom. "You've been wincing all week."

"It's like the string is a knife," Austin said. He held up his fingertips, which were shiny and red at the tips. "I practice at home, and by the end I can barely press anything. Maybe guitar just isn't for me."

Ms. Yoon was tuning a ukulele at the front of the room, but she didn't come over. Instead she nodded toward Mohammad, who was strumming through a chord progression without pausing at all.

"Ask Mohammad how long he's been playing," she said.

"Two years," Mohammad said, not stopping his strumming. "Want to feel something?" He held out his left hand, palm down. Austin pressed a fingertip against Mohammad's index finger. Under the skin there was a hard, smooth patch, like a pebble glued to the pad.

"Whoa. What is that?"

"A callus," Mohammad said, and kept strumming.

Austin turned the idea over while Ms. Yoon called the class to order. A callus was tough skin. Mohammad's fingers had pressed strings thousands of times, and the skin had answered by thickening. Which meant the soreness wasn't a signal to quit. It was a stage, like being bad at a video game before you get good. The pattern was invisible, but the evidence was sitting right there on Mohammad's hand.

He raised his hand. "Ms. Yoon, can I take a practice chart home? Like, a paper one I can mark off?"

"You can make one yourself," she said, and slid a blank transparency sheet and a marker down the table. "Transparent plastic, so you can tape it over your wall calendar and see the days underneath." That clarified the plan for Austin: one box for every day he practiced, and Mohammad promised to text him a reminder each evening.

He played through the whole class, wincing but not stopping. By Friday his chart had seven marks, and the red shine on his fingertips had gone dull and tight.

On Monday, Mohammad picked up Austin's guitar to demonstrate a chord, pressed down, and yanked his hand back. "Ow! These strings feel brand new. Mine are so old they're soft." He laughed and rubbed his thumb. "Guess tough fingers aren't the only thing that matters."

"Give it a week," Austin said. "It worked for me."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
story:
Ella got to the field ten minutes early, but the line at the check-in table already stretched past the bleachers. Ms. Mercado stood at a folding table with a clipboard, and every few seconds somebody walked away from her with a slumped look. Ella watched Kaleb reach the front, say something, and then peel off toward the fence, kicking a cone on the way.

She caught up to him by the water jugs. "What happened?"

"I don't have the form," Kaleb said. "The physical form. Safa didn't bring hers either, and I just saw two eighth graders get turned away for the same thing. The whole tryout is falling apart."

Ella looked back at the table. Ms. Mercado was not checking whether anyone could run or catch; she was checking paper. Safa jogged over, holding her phone out. "Read this. My mom just texted me."

The message said: "Sorry honey, the clinic can't fit you in until next week. Coach won't let you practice without a doctor signing the form, no exceptions." Safa lowered the phone. "I thought the physical was just for the kids who made the team."

"That's what I thought too," Ella said. She counted the players still in line, then counted the ones walking away. Almost half the group was missing. She thought about her own backpack, where her form had sat for three days before she remembered to get it signed. "So nobody's allowed to try out, or even practice, until a doctor or a nurse practitioner has done the checkup and signed. That has to be why they announced it in June and again in August. It's a rule before the rule."

The irony was that Safa had been training all summer and Ella had barely sustained any kind of routine, yet Ella was the one walking onto the grass. "That's not fair," Safa said. "I'm better than half those girls."

"You're better than me, probably," Ella said. "I'm biased about my own catching, so you can't trust my opinion, but still."

Ms. Mercado blew her whistle. "Tryouts start in five minutes. Cleats on, forms in."

Kaleb sat down on the fence rail and pulled out his phone. "There's a walk-in clinic two blocks from school. Safa, your mom said next week at her clinic, but what about the other one?"

Safa stared at him, then at the field, then started running for the parking lot, phone already at her ear. "Tell them to hold my spot," she called back over her shoulder. "I'll be back before the second drill."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Lowering the coverslip onto the slide at an angle, one edge first, helps push out air so fewer bubbles form over the cells.
story:
Levi dreaded fifth period on Tuesdays, because that was microscope lab, and last week he had broken a slide and everyone had heard the crack. Today Mr. Andersen had written a new task on the board: onion skin cells, with a drawing in your notebook showing the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus, all labeled. Levi sat down and pulled the little dish of onion toward him, wondering how anyone was supposed to find one cell, let alone three parts of it, in something as thin as a whisper.

Aicha was already at the next microscope, and she was frowning at her slide. "Look," she said, waving him over. "My cells are so weird. They're just circles, all round and black-rimmed, and they're everywhere." Levi bent to her eyepiece. The field was crowded with dark rings of different sizes, like shadows of coins scattered on a bright floor. He straightened up slowly, thinking. The circles didn't look like the diagram in the textbook, with its neat brick-wall rows. Could a cell really be a perfect empty ring? "Maybe they're not cells at all," he said. "Maybe they're air, trapped somehow." Aicha groaned. "Great. My whole slide is nothing."

Levi went back to his own station and decided to try something. The first time he had made a slide, he had dropped the coverslip flat, straight down, like slamming a lid. He wondered what would happen if he did it differently, lowering one edge first so the glass touched the water at an angle and settled gradually over the drop. He peeled a sliver of onion skin with tweezers, laid it in the drop of water, took a breath, and tilted the coverslip so just its edge touched the slide first. Then he let it ease down, slowly, the way you'd close a door on a sleeping cat.

At the eyepiece, he held still. No black rings. Instead the field was a wall of pale rectangles, row after row of them, like an extravagant palace with a thousand identical windows, or a monarchy of tiny boxes all lined up in ranks. A dot sat near the middle of each one. "Aicha," he called. "Come look." She leaned in, and he heard her breath catch. "Those are the cells? They're actually there?" Mr. Andersen passed behind them and glanced at Levi's notebook, where Levi had already started labeling. He gave a small nod and moved on without a word.

When Aicha remade her slide, she copied Levi's tilt without asking why, one edge first, slow. This time she saw the same pale rows. "So it was the air the whole time," she said, sketching fast before anything could change. "How did you figure that out?" Levi shrugged and turned back to his own eyepiece, adjusting the fine focus until the nucleus in the nearest cell sharpened into a small dark dot. "I dropped the lid on it," he said, "the way you're not supposed to."
